title: 386. Just Enough Hope to Keep You From Leaving
author: bytitleonly
source: The Best Leadership Newsletter Ever (bytitleonly.substack.com), August 31, 2026
summary: This leadership newsletter imports the dating term "breadcrumbing" — giving someone just enough attention to keep them emotionally invested without ever delivering real commitment — into the workplace, arguing it's a common and underdiagnosed management failure. The piece catalogs its typical forms: a promotion perpetually "coming," a raise deferred to the next budget cycle that never arrives, a career-conversation meeting postponed three times running, each crumb calibrated to keep the employee hopeful, working hard, and not interviewing elsewhere. Its sharpest turn is refusing to let the reader stay comfortably in the role of victim: it argues most managers who breadcrumb aren't malicious, they're avoidant, choosing vague reassurance ("I'm working on it") over the harder, more respectful act of telling someone clearly that the promotion or raise isn't coming. The piece frames this avoidance explicitly as cowardice rather than kindness, arguing that leaving the door open when you know it won't open erodes trust more than a direct no would, and closes with a blunt directive: if you can't deliver on something, don't hint at it — tell people clearly so they can make their own choice about whether to stay.
points: Workplace breadcrumbing follows a repeatable pattern: a promotion or raise perpetually "coming," advocacy "behind the scenes" with no visible evidence, and career conversations that keep getting postponed — each crumb calibrated to keep the employee working hard and not job-hunting.

Employees stay not because they're naive but because leaving would mean admitting the time already invested was wasted — the sunk-cost trap makes it hard to distinguish being strung along from simply being impatient.

Most managers who breadcrumb aren't malicious — they avoid the harder, more respectful conversation of telling someone a promotion or raise genuinely isn't happening, and default to vague reassurance instead.
The piece reframes "leaving the door open" as cowardice rather than kindness: every vague reassurance that strings someone along erodes trust more than a direct, honest no would.

The prescribed fix is specificity: if a promotion or raise isn't coming, say so plainly — being clear and honest, even when uncomfortable, is framed as more respectful than the false hope of continued crumbs.
quotes: It means when someone is giving you just enough attention to keep you emotionally invested, but not enough for any actual commitment. It's not ghosting. Breadcrumbing is worse. The person doesn't disappear. Instead, they drop just enough crumbs of interest to keep you waiting.

Each crumb keeps you hopeful. Each crumb keeps you working harder. And, more importantly, each crumb keeps you from interviewing somewhere else. You're not wrong to feel strung along. You are being strung along.

You don't breadcrumb others because you want to hurt them. You breadcrumb them because you don't want to have the hard conversation. You don't want to tell them the reality that the promotion isn't going to happen.
You think you're being kind by leaving the door open. You're not. You're being a coward. With every conversation that strings them along, you're eroding trust.
If you were actually kind, you'd be telling them the truth. That way they can make their own choice about what to do.

If you can't deliver on something, don't hint at it. If a promotion isn't coming, say it. Tell them that the thing they really want isn't going to happen anytime soon. Be specific. Be honest. Be clear.
